helicoprion:eswiki:6.title: Helicoprion (Naturaleza de la espiral de los dientes)

facts.statement: Helicoprion lived during the Cisuralian to Guadalupian stages of the Permian period.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Cisuralian to Guadalupian (Artinskian to Roadian),

facts.statement: The genus Helicoprion was first described by Alexander Karpinsky in 1899.
facts.quote: authority: Karpinsky, 1899

facts.statement: The type species of the genus Helicoprion is Helicoprion bessonowi.
facts.quote: type_species: Helicoprion bessonowi

facts.statement: Two other recognized species are Helicoprion davisii and Helicoprion ergassaminon.
facts.quote: subdivision: *H. davisii (Woodward, 1886) H. ergassaminon Bendix-Almgreen, 1966

facts.statement: Helicoprion was a large cartilaginous fish that lived approximately 290 to 270 million years ago.
facts.quote: Helicoprion is an extinct genus of large shark-like cartilaginous fish that lived from the Early to the Middle Permian, about 290-270 million years ago.

facts.statement: Helicoprion belongs to the extinct order Eugeneodontiformes within the clade Holocephali, which today only includes chimaeras.
facts.quote: Helicoprion is a member of the Eugeneodontiformes, an extinct order of cartilaginous fish within the clade Holocephali, a group today represented only by chimaeras.

facts.statement: Helicoprion is primarily known from its unique fused, spiral-shaped tooth whorls.
facts.quote: Helicoprion is mainly known from its fused, spiral-shaped tooth whorls, which account for almost all documented fossils of the taxon.

facts.statement: Studies suggest the tooth whorls were located in the lower jaw and used for grasping and slicing soft-bodied prey like cephalopods.
facts.quote: studies based on specimens preserving jaw cartilage indicate that they were positioned in the lower jaw and were specialised for grasping and slicing soft-bodied prey such as cephalopods.

facts.statement: Helicoprion is estimated to have grown between 5 and 12 meters in length.
facts.quote: Helicoprion is estimated to have reached lengths between 5 and 12 m

facts.statement: Helicoprion likely had an external appearance similar to tunas, swordfish, or mackerel sharks.
facts.quote: with a general external appearance possibly comparable to that of tunas, swordfish, or mackerel sharks.

facts.statement: Helicoprion was a pelagic species with a worldwide distribution found in marine deposits.
facts.quote: Fossils of Helicoprion are known from marine deposits worldwide, indicating that it was pelagic and had a cosmopolitan distribution.

facts.statement: The first known Helicoprion specimen preserved a partial tooth whorl with 15 teeth, 14 of which are visible.
facts.quote: The first known specimen of Helicoprion consists of a partial tooth whorl preserving 15 teeth, 14 of which are visible.

facts.statement: The first Helicoprion fossil was discovered in Western Australia by an unnamed gold prospector named Mr. Davis.
facts.quote: It was discovered in Western Australia in a tributary of the Gascoyne River by a gold prospector named Mr. Davis, his first name being unknown.

facts.statement: Henry Woodward initially described the first specimen as Edestus davisii in 1886.
facts.quote: In a 1886 publication, Woodward finally described the specimen as representing a new species of Edestus, which he named Edestus davisii in honor of its discoverer.

facts.statement: More complete tooth whorls were found in the late 19th century by Alexander G. Bessonov near Krasnoufimsk in Russia.
facts.quote: More complete tooth whorls were discovered in the late 19th century by Alexander G. Bessonov of the Russian Academy of Sciences, in a quarry near the town of Krasnoufimsk in Sverdlovsk Oblast.

facts.statement: Alexander Karpinsky first described the Russian fossils in 1899, establishing the new genus Helicoprion.
facts.quote: He sent them to geologist Alexander Karpinsky, who first described them in a monograph published in Russian in 1899, followed later that year by a German translation.

facts.statement: The most complete specimen described by Karpinsky was designated the lectotype by Dmitry Obruchev in 1964.
facts.quote: Among the six specimens described by Karpinsky, the most complete of them, later catalogued as TsNIGR 1/1865 in the collections of the Central Research Geological Museum in Saint Petersburg, was designated as the lectotype by Russian paleontologist Dmitry Obruchev in a 1964 publication.

facts.statement: The lectotype specimen was stolen in 1998 and later recovered by David J. Ward.
facts.quote: This same specimen was stolen in 1998 and was eventually recovered by British paleontologist David J. Ward with the assistance of an anonymous fossil dealer.

facts.statement: Helicoprion ergassaminon was described in 1966 by Svend Erik Bendix-Almgreen based on fossils from Idaho.
facts.quote: H. ergassaminon was first described in 1966 by Danish ichthyologist Svend Erik Bendix-Almgreen in a monograph devoted to several Helicoprion fossils housed in the paleontological collections of various universities in Idaho, USA.

facts.statement: The holotype of H. ergassaminon, nicknamed "Idaho 5", was discovered in a mine near Fort Hall and originally reported to be at the University of Idaho.
facts.quote: This latter, nicknamed "Idaho 5" and discovered in a now-abandoned mine near Fort Hall, was reported by Bendix-Almgreen to be stored at the University of Idaho in Moscow, Idaho.

facts.statement: The holotype of H. ergassaminon was rediscovered in 2017 and moved to Idaho State University in 2023.
facts.quote: The holotype was finally rediscovered in 2017 during the recataloguing of the fossil collections at the Natural History Museum of Denmark, before being transferred in 2023 to the Idaho State University in Pocatello, where it is now held.

facts.statement: Charles R. Eastman challenged Karpinsky's classification of H. davisii in 1902, placing it in the genus Campyloprion.
facts.quote: However, this interpretation was challenged as early as 1902 by American paleontologist Charles R. Eastman, who assigned the species to Campyloprion, a newly erected and closely related taxon.

facts.statement: Karpinsky maintained his original classification of H. davisii as Helicoprion, a view supported by later authors.
facts.quote: In later publications, Karpinsky reaffirmed the position he had argued in 1899, an interpretation followed by several authors in the subsequent decades.

facts.statement: Hay described the species Lissoprion ferrieri in 1907 and 1909 based on fossils found in phosphate deposits along the Idaho–Wyoming border.
facts.quote: In his 1907 and 1909 works, Hay erected a new genus and species of eugeneodont, Lissoprion ferrieri, which he described from three fossil specimens originating from phosphate deposits along the Idaho–Wyoming border.

facts.statement: Karpinsky reclassified the taxon as H. ferrieri in 1911.
facts.quote: Karpinsky to reclassify the taxon as H. ferrieri in 1911

facts.statement: Harry E. Wheeler named the species H. sierrensis and H. nevadensis in 1939 based on fossils from California and Nevada.
facts.quote: In 1939, American geologist Harry E. Wheeler named two additional Helicoprion species, H. sierrensis and H. nevadensis, based on type specimens from California and Nevada, respectively.

facts.statement: Federico K. G. Müllerried described the species H. mexicanus in 1945 based on a partial tooth whorl with 10 teeth found in Coahuila, Mexico.
facts.quote: In 1945, geologist Federico K. G. Müllerried described the species H. mexicanus on the basis of a poorly preserved partial tooth whorl bearing 10 teeth, discovered in the Mexican state of Coahuila.

facts.statement: Obruchev illustrated a poorly preserved fossil specimen with two teeth in 1953, found in the Ural Mountains of Russia.
facts.quote: In 1953, Obruchev illustrated in his monograph a poorly preserved fossil specimen preserving the impression and root of two teeth, discovered in the Ural Mountains of Russia.

facts.statement: Stanisław Siedlecki named the species H. svalis in 1970 based on fossils from the Norwegian archipelago of Svalbard.
facts.quote: In 1970, Polish geologist Stanisław Siedlecki named the species H. svalis on the basis of isolated teeth and fragmentary tooth whorls recovered from the Norwegian archipelago of Svalbard.

facts.statement: Tapanila and Pruitt noted in 2013 that the H. jingmenense specimen was partially obscured, likely leading to an underestimation of tooth height.
facts.quote: In their 2013 revision, though, Tapanila and Pruitt pointed out that the specimen is partially obscured by its surrounding matrix, which likely led to an underestimation of tooth height.

facts.statement: Eastman concluded in 1903 that Campyloprion was similar enough to Helicoprion to be reassigned as a lineage within that genus.
facts.quote: In 1903, shortly after establishing Campyloprion with C. annectans as its type species, Eastman apparently concluded that this taxon was sufficiently similar to Helicoprion to be reassigned as a distinct lineage within that genus.

facts.statement: Hay reassigned C. lecontei and C. davisii to the genus Toxoprion in his 1909 publication.
facts.quote: In his 1909 publication, Hay kept Helicoprion and Campyloprion separate, but nevertheless reassigned C. lecontei and C. davisii to the newly erected genus Toxoprion, with the former designated as its type species.

facts.statement: Karpinsky erected the species H. clerci in 1916 based on fossils found near Krasnoufimsk.
facts.quote: In 1916, Karpinsky erected the species H. clerci on the basis of fragmentary remains of a large tooth whorl discovered near Krasnoufimsk, the same locality that yielded the original fossils of H. bessonowi.

facts.statement: Dagmar Merino-Rodo and Philippe Janvier described the species P. mariosuarezi in 1986 based on fossils near La Paz, Bolivia.
facts.quote: In 1986, the Bolivian geologist Dagmar Merino-Rodo and the French paleontologist Philippe Janvier described a second species, P. mariosuarezi, based on fossils unearthed near La Paz, Bolivia.

facts.statement: Oleg Lebedev and colleagues reclassified the species into the genus Karpinskiprion in 2022.
facts.quote: In 2022, Russian palaeontologist Oleg Lebedev and colleagues once again reclassified the species into its own genus, which they named Karpinskiprion.

facts.statement: Helicoprion had a skeleton made of cartilage like other chondrichthyan fish.
facts.quote: Like other chondrichthyan fish, Helicoprion had a skeleton made of cartilage.

facts.statement: Eugeneodonts had a streamlined, torpedo-shaped body with triangular pectoral fins.
facts.quote: Eugeneodonts are characterized by a fusiform (streamlined, torpedo-shaped) body plan, with triangular pectoral fins.

facts.statement: Eugeneodonts had a single large triangular dorsal fin without a spine and a tall, forked caudal fin that appeared homocercal.
facts.quote: They have a single large and triangular dorsal fin without a fin spine, and a tall, forked caudal fin, which externally appears to be homocercal (with two equally sized lobes).

facts.statement: Eugeneodonts lacked pelvic and anal fins, and Romerodus had broad keels along its body up to the tail.
facts.quote: Eugeneodonts also lack pelvic and anal fins, and the genus Romerodus had broad keels along the side of the body up to the caudal fin.

facts.statement: Lebedev suggested in 2009 that Helicoprion individuals with 35-40 cm tooth whorls could reach 5-8 meters in length.
facts.quote: Based on the proportional size of caseodontoid tooth whorls, Lebedev suggested in 2009 that Helicoprion individuals with tooth whorls 35 - 40 cm in diameter could reach 5 - 8 m in total length, comparable to the size of modern basking sharks.

facts.statement: The largest known Helicoprion tooth whorl, IMNH 49382, measured 56 cm in diameter and 14 cm in height, belonging to an individual at least 7 meters long.
facts.quote: The largest known Helicoprion tooth whorl, specimen IMNH 49382, reached 56 cm in diameter and 14 cm in crown height, and would have belonged to an individual 7 m or more in length.

facts.statement: Tapanila suggested that the largest Helicoprion individuals could have reached 9.7-12 meters in length.
facts.quote: Tapanila has suggested a total length of 9.7-12 m for the largest Helicoprion individuals.

facts.statement: Naugolnykh and Naumkin proposed in 2018 and 2023 that Parahelicoprion might be a junior synonym of Helicoprion.
facts.quote: In 2018 and 2023, Russian palaeontologists Sergey V. Naugolnykh and Dmitry V. Naumkin proposed that Parahelicoprion may, in fact, represent a junior synonym of Helicoprion, suggesting that the genus may have been named on the basis of fossils belonging to exceptionally large and old individuals of the latter.

facts.statement: Some authors continue to consider Parahelicoprion distinct from Helicoprion.
facts.quote: Other authors have continued to consider the genus to be distinct from Helicoprion.

facts.statement: Lebedev and colleagues reclassified the species into the genus Karpinskiprion in 2022.
facts.quote: However, in 2022, Russian palaeontologist Oleg Lebedev and colleagues once again reclassified the species into its own genus, which they named Karpinskiprion.

facts.statement: Most Helicoprion fossils consist of a spiral-shaped root holding dozens of enameloid teeth arranged in a logarithmic spiral.
facts.quote: Almost all Helicoprion specimens are known solely from "tooth whorls", which consist of dozens of enameloid-covered teeth embedded within a single logarithmic spiral-shaped root.

facts.statement: The largest teeth in the Helicoprion spiral whorl could exceed 10 centimeters in height.
facts.quote: Tooth size increases away from the center of the spiral, with the largest teeth possibly exceeding 10 cm in height.

facts.statement: The three known species of Helicoprion are distinguished solely by differences in their tooth whorl anatomy.
facts.quote: The three species of Helicoprion differ only in the anatomy of their tooth whorls.

facts.statement: Helicoprion davisii is identified by tall, widely spaced tooth crowns with tips that curve forward.
facts.quote: H. davisii can be differentiated from other Helicoprion species by tall, widely spaced tooth crowns with forward-curved tooth tips.

facts.statement: Helicoprion bessonowi possessed short, closely spaced teeth with backward-curving tips and widely angled bases.
facts.quote: H. bessonowi had comparatively short, closely spaced tooth crowns, backward-curved teeth, a narrow shaft, and widely angled tooth bases.

facts.statement: CT scans of the best-preserved specimen revealed nearly complete upper and lower jaws preserved in three-dimensional articulation.
facts.quote: CT scanning revealed a nearly complete set of upper and lower jaws, still in articulation and preserved in three dimensions.

facts.statement: The best-preserved Helicoprion specimen lacks the chondrocranium, the cartilage structure that would have held the brain and sensory organs.
facts.quote: The specimen does not preserve a chondrocranium, the cartilaginous structure that would have housed the brain and sensory organs.

facts.statement: Helicoprion possessed an autodiastylic jaw suspension where the upper jaw was attached to the skull at two separate points without fusion.
facts.quote: Helicoprion had an autodiastylic jaw suspension, meaning that the inner edge of the palatoquadrate was firmly attached (but not fused) to the chondrocranium at two separate points.

facts.statement: A unique extra projection on Helicoprion's lower jaw likely prevented the tooth whorl from puncturing the skull during jaw closure.
facts.quote: The Meckel's cartilage of Helicoprion has an additional projection right before the joint with the palatoquadrate. This extra process, unique to Helicoprion, likely served to limit jaw closure to prevent the whorl from puncturing the skull.

facts.statement: Specialized labial cartilage provided lateral support for the tooth whorl and widened near the roots of each spiral revolution.
facts.quote: The labial cartilage provides lateral support for the tooth whorl, widening near the root of each revolution.

facts.statement: Tooth-like scales called odontodes have been found associated with Helicoprion bessonowi fossils in Kazakhstan.
facts.quote: Tooth-like chondrichthyan scales, specifically known as odontodes, have been found associated with H. bessonowi remains in Kazakhstan.

facts.statement: Helicoprion scales were more sharply pointed than those of other eugeneodonts.
facts.quote: Compared to other eugeneodonts, the scales of Helicoprion are more strongly pointed.

facts.statement: Skull characteristics confirm that Helicoprion belongs to the chondrichthyan subclass Holocephali.
facts.quote: Skull data from IMNH 37899 reveal several characteristics, such as an autodiastylic (two-jointed) jaw suspension with a nonsuspensory hyomandibula, which confirm the placement of Helicoprion within the chondrichthyan subclass Holocephali (or the more broadly defined Euchondrocephali).

facts.statement: Helicoprion is classified as a member of the order Eugeneodontiformes, defined by midline tooth whorls and autodiastylic skulls.
facts.quote: Helicoprion can be characterized as a member of Eugeneodontiformes, an order of holocephalans that lived from the Devonian to Triassic periods and are defined by their tooth whorls along the midline of the jaw and autodiastylic skulls.

facts.statement: Helicoprionidae members are distinguished by large, cartilage-supported tooth whorls that added new teeth continuously at the spiral's apex.
facts.quote: Members of this family are distinguished by their large, strongly arched tooth whorls supported by cartilage, which do not replace teeth, but instead add new ones continuously at the apex of the spiral, with tooth bases inclined forward.

facts.statement: Helicoprion is unique in its family for having a complete, multi-revolution spiral whorl, unlike the incomplete spirals of other genera.
facts.quote: Helicoprion is unique among members of its family in possessing a closed (complete) spiral whorl, which revolves around itself multiple times, while the tooth whorls of other genera form an incomplete, open spiral.

facts.statement: Helicoprion jaws were extensively laterally compressed, though this may be partly due to fossil compression artifacts.
facts.quote: The jaws are extensively laterally compressed (narrow) compared to living chondrichthyans, though this may at least partially be an artifact of compression after death.

facts.statement: The upper jaw of Helicoprion was lined with small, low, rounded teeth that formed a pavement scraping against the main tooth whorl.
facts.quote: The inner surface of the palatoquadrate was covered with numerous small (~2 mm wide) teeth. The palatoquadrate teeth were low and rounded, forming a "pavement" that scraped against the tooth whorl.

facts.statement: The labial cartilage wedged into the upper jaw to distribute forces and limit jaw closure.
facts.quote: By wedging into the palatoquadrate while the mouth is closed, the upper edge of the labial cartilage helps to spread out the forces used to limit the extent of the jaw closure.

facts.statement: The order Eugeneodontiformes, to which Helicoprion belongs, lived from the Devonian to the Triassic periods.
facts.quote: Eugeneodontiformes, an order of holocephalans that lived from the Devonian to Triassic periods and are defined by their tooth whorls along the midline of the jaw and autodiastylic skulls.

facts.statement: A 2015 biomechanical study suggests Helicoprion's spiral teeth had different functions based on their position in the whorl.
facts.quote: Biomechanical modelling in a 2015 paper by American biologist Jason B. Ramsay and colleagues suggests that the teeth in the whorl had distinct functions depending on where they were in the spiral.

facts.statement: Research indicates the front teeth snagged prey, middle teeth speared it, and hind teeth punctured it to push it into the throat.
facts.quote: The foremost teeth served to snag and pull prey further into the mouth, while the middle teeth speared, and the hind teeth punctured and brought prey further into the throat.

facts.statement: During feeding, Helicoprion squeezed prey between its tooth whorl and the palatoquadrate bones.
facts.quote: The prey would be squeezed between the whorl and the palatoquadrates during feeding.

facts.statement: The saw-like tooth arrangement and lack of tooth wear suggest Helicoprion ate soft-bodied prey rather than hard-shelled organisms.
facts.quote: The unusual, saw-like tooth whorl and the lack of wear on the teeth of Helicoprion implies a diet of soft-bodied prey, as hard-shelled prey would simply slip out of the mouth.

facts.statement: Helicoprion likely captured prey with rapid jaw closures and then used repeated opening and closing motions to saw through it.
facts.quote: Helicoprion likely used a series of rapid, forceful jaw closures to initially capture and push prey deeper into the mouth, followed by repeated opening and closing of the jaw to saw through prey.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest the tooth whorl was an effective tool for extracting soft bodies from hard-shelled cephalopods like ammonoids and nautiloids.
facts.quote: Ramsay and colleagues further suggested that the whorl could have served as an effective mechanism for shelling hard-shelled cephalopods such as ammonoids and nautiloids, which were abundant in Early Permian oceans.

facts.statement: Estimates place Helicoprion's bite force between 1,192 and 2,391 Newtons with bite stresses between 397 and 797 million Newtons per square meter.
facts.quote: At the three points of contact, the estimated bite force ranges between 1,192 and 2,391 N, with estimated bite stresses ranging from 397 to 797 e6N/m2 during prey contact.

facts.statement: Its high bite force suggests Helicoprion may have been capable of eating vertebrates in addition to cephalopods.
facts.quote: Due to its high bite force, Helicoprion may have also been able to eat vertebrates, in addition to cephalopods.

facts.statement: In 1886, Woodward described H. davisii while it was still assigned to the genus Edestus and discussed various interpretations of the fossils.
facts.quote: In his original 1886 description of H. davisii, then assigned to Edestus, Woodward discussed the various interpretations that had been proposed regarding the nature of the fossils placed in that genus.

facts.statement: Karpinsky established the genus Helicoprion in 1899, noting the tooth whorl's peculiar nature made determining its function difficult.
facts.quote: When Karpinsky erected the genus Helicoprion in 1899, he emphasized that the peculiar nature of the tooth whorl made it difficult to draw precise conclusions about its function.

facts.statement: Karpinsky suggested the whorl curled forward from the upper jaw for defense or offense, a view supported by comparisons to Edestus jaw structures re-evaluated in 1899.
facts.quote: He cautiously suggested that it may have curled forward from the upper jaw for defensive or offensive purposes, an idea supported by comparison with the upper dental blades of Edestus, which by 1899 had been re-evaluated as structures belonging to the jaw.

facts.statement: Eastman supported the hypothesis that the whorl was a defensive structure on the body rather than part of the mouth, despite similarities to other chondrichthyan teeth.
facts.quote: Though Eastman admitted that the teeth of the whorl were very similar to those of other chondrichthyans, he still supported the idea that the whorl may have been a defensive structure embedded into the body of the animal, rather than the mouth.

facts.statement: Ernest Van Den Broeck argued the whorl was likely a paired oral apparatus inside the cheeks due to its fragility.
facts.quote: The Belgian paleontologist Ernest Van Den Broeck emphasized the fragility of the structure and argued that it would be better protected if it were a paired oral apparatus located within the animal's cheeks.

facts.statement: Reconstructions similar to Karpinsky's 1899 proposals appeared in Russian publications and textbooks as late as 2001.
facts.quote: Reconstructions similar to those proposed by Karpinsky in 1899 continued to appear in Russian publications and textbooks as late as 2001.

facts.statement: By the mid-20th century, paleontologists generally accepted that the tooth whorl of Helicoprion was located in the lower jaw.
facts.quote: By the mid-20th century, the tooth whorl was generally accepted to be positioned in the lower jaw.

facts.statement: In 1966, Bendix-Almgreen reinterpreted the tooth whorl as a symphyseal structure wedged between Meckelian cartilages at the front of the jaw.
facts.quote: In his 1966 publication, Bendix-Almgreen reinterpreted the tooth whorl of Helicoprion as a symphyseal structure wedged between the meckelian cartilages, which were separated by a gap at the front.

facts.statement: In 2008, paleoartist Mary Parrish created a reconstruction placing the tooth whorl deeper within the throat for the Smithsonian Museum of Natural History.
facts.quote: In 2008, American paleoartist Mary Parrish created a new reconstruction for the renovated Ocean Hall at the Smithsonian Museum of Natural History.

facts.statement: More than half of the Helicoprion fossils belong to the species H. davisii, primarily found in the Phosphoria Formation in Idaho.
facts.quote: More than half of the fossils assigned to the genus belong to H. davisii, primarily recovered from the Phosphoria Formation in Idaho.

facts.statement: Approximately 25% of Helicoprion fossils represent the species H. bessonowi, known from the Divya Formation in the Ural Mountains of Russia.
facts.quote: Approximately 25% represent H. bessonowi, known from the Divya Formation in the Ural Mountains of Russia.

facts.statement: Helicoprion fossils have been found in geographically dispersed deposits worldwide, including Australia, Canada, China, Kazakhstan, Japan, Laos, Mexico, and Norway.
facts.quote: Other specimens come from more geographically dispersed deposits worldwide, including additional U.S. states as well as Australia, Canada, China, Kazakhstan, Japan, Laos, Mexico, and Norway.

facts.statement: Helicoprion's diet likely consisted primarily of cephalopods like belemnoids, nautiloids, and ammonoids, and it may have also hunted cartilaginous and unarmored bony fish.
facts.quote: The genus' diet likely consisted primarily of cephalopods such as belemnoids, nautiloids and ammonoids, and it also may have hunted cartilaginous and unarmored bony fish as well.

facts.statement: The extinction of Helicoprion is not associated with a major extinction event and is suggested to have been a background extinction.
facts.quote: The disappearance of Helicoprion is not associated with a larger extinction event, and has been suggested to have been a background extinction.

facts.statement: The genus Helicoprion was described by Karpinsky in 1899.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Karpinsky, 1899

facts.statement: Helicoprion is classified within the class Chondrichthyes.
facts.quote: classis: Chondrichthyes

facts.statement: Helicoprion belongs to the order Eugeneodontiformes.
facts.quote: ordo: Eugeneodontiformes

facts.statement: Helicoprion is part of the family Agassizodontidae.
facts.quote: familia: Agassizodontidae

facts.statement: Helicoprion first appeared in the Lower Carboniferous oceans about 280 million years ago, survived the Permian-Triassic extinction, and went extinct in the Late Triassic about 225 million years ago.
facts.quote: Helicoprion (gr. "sierra en espiral") es un género extinto de peces cartilaginosos del orden Eugeneodontiformes, similar a los tiburones que surgió por primera vez en los océanos del Carbonífero inferior (hace unos 280 millones de años) y sobrevivió a la extinción masiva del Pérmico-Triásico, y terminó extinguiéndose en el Triásico Superior hace unos 225 millones de años.

facts.statement: The only known fossil remains of Helicoprion were teeth arranged in a spiral resembling a circular saw.
facts.quote: Los únicos restos fósiles conocidos eran los dientes, ordenados en una fantástica espiral que recuerda mucho una sierra circular.

facts.statement: Comparisons with other eugeneodontids suggest Helicoprion may have reached a length of about 7 meters.
facts.quote: Al compararlo con otros eugeneodóntidos, se piensa que el Helicoprion pudo haber alcanzado una talla de unos 7 metros de largo.

facts.statement: The sharp teeth of Helicoprion imply that these animals were carnivores.
facts.quote: Los dientes eran afilados, lo que implica que estos animales eran carnívoros.

facts.statement: A hypothesis suggests Helicoprion fed on ammonites and that its teeth were specialized for breaking their shells.
facts.quote: Una hipótesis es que se alimentaba de ammonites y que sus dientes estaban especializados en la tarea de romper los caparazones de estos animales.

facts.statement: It is debated whether the tooth whorl functioned like a sawfish snout for incapacitating prey via lateral blows.
facts.quote: The utility of the tooth whorl in this type of reconstruction was inferred based on sawfish, which incapacitate prey using lateral blows of their denticle-covered snouts.

facts.statement: The hypothesis that the tooth whorl assisted swallowing is debated due to criticism regarding the structure's potential ineffectiveness.
facts.quote: This reconstruction was criticized for the overly intricate and potentially ineffective design of such a structure, if solely used to assist swallowing.

facts.statement: Helicoprion fossils first appeared in Late Carboniferous marine strata, flourished during the Permian, and disappeared from the record by the Early Triassic.
facts.quote: Los fósiles de las especies de Helicoprion aparecieron por primera vez en los estratos marinos del Carbonífero Superior, proliferando en gran medida durante el Pérmico, y desaparecen del registro durante el Triásico Inferior.

facts.statement: Helicoprion fossils have been found in the Ural Mountains, the Wandagee Mountains of Western Australia, China, and western North America including the Canadian Arctic and states like New Mexico, Idaho, Nevada, Wyoming, Texas, Utah, and California.
facts.quote: Sus fósiles se han encontrado en los Montes Urales, en los Montes Wandagee de Australia Occidental, en China junto con los géneros relacionados Sinohelicoprion y Hunanohelicoprion, y en el oeste de América del Norte, incluyendo el Ártico canadiense, los estados de Nuevo México, Idaho, Nevada, Wyoming, Texas, Utah y California.

facts.statement: Based on fossil locations, it is speculated that Helicoprion species lived along the southwestern coast of Gondwana and later that of Pangea.
facts.quote: Dadas las ubicaciones de los fósiles, se especula que las distintas especies de Helicoprion vivían en la costa suroccidental de Gondwana, y más tarde, la de Pangea.

facts.statement: Until recently, the only known fossils of this species were teeth organized in a 'tooth spiral' resembling a circular saw.
facts.quote: Hasta hace poco, los únicos fósiles conocidos de esta especie fueron los dientes, que se organizaban en una «espiral de dientes» que recuerda mucho a una sierra circular.

facts.statement: It was not until the discovery of the skull of a related shark genus, Ornithoprion, that it became evident that the spiral tooth set was located in the lower jaw.
facts.quote: No fue sino hasta el descubrimiento del cráneo de un género relacionado de tiburón Ornithoprion, cuando se hizo evidente que el conjunto de dientes en espiral se situaba en la mandíbula inferior.

facts.statement: The tooth-whorl grouped all teeth produced by an individual in the lower jaw, and as the individual grew, new teeth were produced that pushed older teeth toward the center of the spiral.
facts.quote: El diente-verticilo agrupaba todos los dientes producidos por un individuo en la mandíbula inferior, y a medida que el individuo crecía, se producían nuevos dientes que desplazaban hacia el centro de la espiral a los más viejos.

facts.statement: A 2008 reconstruction by Mary Parrish, Robert Purdy, Víctor Springer, and Matt Carrano for the Smithsonian places the tooth-whorl deepest in the throat, though other studies have not accepted this conclusion.
facts.quote: Una reconstrucción de 2008, creado por Mary Parrish bajo la dirección de Robert Purdy, Víctor Springer y Matt Carrano para el Smithsonian, coloca el verticilo más profundo en la garganta, aunque otros estudios no han aceptado esta conclusión.

facts.statement: A 2013 study based on new data places the tooth-whorl at the back of the jaw, where it would occupy the entire mandibular arch.
facts.quote: Un estudio de 2013 sobre la base de nuevos datos coloca el diente-verticilo en la parte posterior de la mandíbula, en la que el diente-verticilo ocuparía todo el arco mandibular.

facts.statement: Although no complete Helicoprion skulls exist, the fact that related shark species had long, pointed snouts suggests Helicoprion may have possessed one as well.
facts.quote: Si bien no hay cráneos completos de Helicoprion, el hecho de que las especies relacionadas de tiburones tenían hocicos largos en punta sugiere que Helicoprion pudo también poseerlo así.
